paras: The threatened lynching of Press Sams was the reported flight of Press Sams, a Black hired man described in the papers as a "mulatto" and a "negro," from would-be lynchers near Moscow, Kentucky, in late September 1888, after he eloped with and married Hattie Flack, the white daughter of a St. Louis commission merchant. A deputy sheriff from Jacksonville, Illinois, tracked the couple to Kentucky and brought Flack back to her family, while wire reports said Sams "fled to escape lynching." One dispatch said the deputy hinted that Sams had been lynched, but other accounts said he escaped or left the country.

Hattie Flack, reported as eighteen or nineteen years old, was the daughter of Charles E. Flack of a St. Louis commission firm. Sams worked for the family near Jacksonville, in Morgan County, Illinois, and was described either as her father's coachman or as a hired man on his farm. Brief reports in mid-September said the two had eloped on a Saturday night and married.

Deputy Sheriff D. C. McCoy, a friend of the Flack family, left Jacksonville in late September on Sams's trail. According to a dispatch dated at Clinton, Kentucky, Flack was arrested at Moscow on a Saturday night in the house of Jim Gholson, described as Sams's brother-in-law, and refused to go with the officers until she learned they held a warrant for her. The Philadelphia Press special instead placed the couple at a log cabin "in the mountains, near Clinton," with the family of Sams's brother-in-law, and said Flack agreed to leave only after McCoy convinced her that Sams had another wife from whom he had never been divorced.

McCoy reached St. Louis with Flack on October 1 and turned her over to her father. The St. Louis wire of that day reported that "Sams fled to escape lynching" and that he had been a married man when he wed Flack. The Clinton dispatch, by contrast, said only that Sams "has since deserted her" and did not mention any threat.

A St. Louis item in the Rock Island Argus described Sams as "a horse thief" and "a fugitive in Kentucky." Later briefs repeated that he had fled from Moscow "to escape lynchers," and the Columbia Banner of Magnolia, Arkansas, wrote that he "made his escape, or he would have been lynched." No report of Sams's capture, of a bigamy charge, of an inquest, or of any action against those said to have threatened him was found in the coverage.

The St. Louis wire of October 1 ran in Memphis, Omaha and other cities and reappeared later in the month in weekly news columns in Dakota and Kansas. Headlines treated it as a scandal of a white daughter's choice: "Tired of Her Negro Husband" in the Omaha Bee, "She Repents Her Folly" in the Memphis Appeal, "Miss Flack's Infatuation" in the Annapolis Evening Capital, and "Wasn't Even an Honest Negro" in the Rock Island Argus, which also called Sams "a notorious negro."

The Washington Evening Star, reprinting the Philadelphia Press special, headed it "He Has Probably Been Lynched," and the Sacramento Record-Union ran a California Associated Press version under "The Color Line. Alleged Lynching of a Negro Who Eloped with a White Girl." The Star printed without comment McCoy's hint that Sams was lynched "to save the state the expense of his trial for bigamy," alongside the Clinton report that he had left the country.

In a column of news for Black readers, the Cleveland Gazette reported the elopement before the Kentucky arrest as a Jacksonville "social sensation," naming the groom as "John Sams, a coal black Negro" with "some education and considerable natural shrewdness." The Western Appeal of St. Paul reprinted the Clinton dispatch in its column of news "Pertaining to Colored People," writing "a Colored man" where the original read "a negro," and its version carried no word of lynching.

Accounts differed on what became of Sams: according to the Philadelphia Press special, McCoy refused to say but "intimates that he was lynched," while the same dispatch gave the Clinton report that Sams had left the country. The wire and later briefs said he fled, and the Rock Island item called him a fugitive; the hint of a killing came from the pursuing deputy alone and was not confirmed in any report found.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Press Sams
bases: Wire reports said Sams, a Black man who had married a white woman, 'fled to escape lynching' and one dispatch said the deputy hinted he had been lynched (A4, A8, A16).

Only the deputy's unconfirmed hint, relayed in one special dispatch, suggests Sams was killed, while the Clinton report and the wire say he left the country or fled (A4, A8, A3); no report names or describes any mob, so a killing by a group cannot be established.
Several independent dispatches agree that Flack was recovered near Moscow and Sams escaped (A3, A6, A8), but the Philadelphia Press special relays the deputy's hint that he was lynched (A4).

framing.detail: The Philadelphia Press special, headed 'He Has Probably Been Lynched', passed on the deputy's hint of a lynching to spare the cost of a bigamy trial without comment.
The St. Louis wire ran under headlines of female folly ('She Repents Her Folly', 'Tired of Her Negro Husband') and said Sams 'induced' Flack to wed him.
The Rock Island Argus headed its item 'Wasn't Even an Honest Negro' and called Sams 'a notorious negro' and a horse thief.
The Sacramento Record-Union ran the story as 'The Color Line. Alleged Lynching of a Negro Who Eloped with a White Girl.'
The Western Appeal of St. Paul printed the Clinton dispatch in a column of news 'Pertaining to Colored People', writing 'a Colored man' where the original had 'a negro'.
